tip: гораздо (garazda = much) intensifies a comparative: гораздо интереснее (garazda interesnee = much more interesting).
After a comparative, the thing compared can go in the genitive: важнее работы (vazhnee raboty = more important than work).
работать (rabotat = to work) plus the instrumental names a job: работает врачом (rabotaet vrachom = works as a doctor).
Numbers 2, 3, 4 take a genitive singular noun: три комнаты (tri komnaty = three rooms), not the plural form.
For equal comparison use такой же ... как (takoy zhe ... kak = as ... as): такой же высокий (takoy zhe vysokiy = just as tall).
которую (katoruyu = that/which) is feminine accusative here, matching книга (kniga = book) as the object being read.
With one subject, чтобы (chtoby = in order to) takes the infinitive: чтобы успеть (chtoby uspet = in order to make it).
Negative commands usually take the imperfective verb: не сдавайся (ne sdavaysya = don't give up), not the perfective form.
When the comparison is a whole clause, use чем (chem = than): сильнее, чем выглядит (silnee, chem vyglyadit = stronger than she looks).
более (bolee = more) plus a plain adjective forms a comparative: более опытный (bolee opytnyy = more experienced).
самый (samyy = most) before an adjective builds the superlative: самый высокий (samyy vysokiy = the tallest).
The по- prefix on a comparative softens it to 'a bit more': поудобнее (paudobnee = a bit more comfortable).
A comparative plus всех (vsekh = than all) means best of the group: быстрее всех (bystree vsekh = faster than everyone).
The frame чем ... тем ... (chem ... tem ... = the more ... the more) links two comparatives: чем дальше, тем больше (chem dalshe, tem bolshe).
по-русски (pa-russki = in Russian) is the set adverb for speaking a language: говорит по-русски (gavarit pa-russki = speaks Russian).
To say someone is absent, use нет plus the genitive: меня нет (menya net = I'm not here, I'm away).
Many comparatives change their last stem sound: короткий becomes короче (karotkiy to karoche = shorter), the т turning into ч.
уже (uzhe = narrower) looks exactly like уже meaning already; stress and context tell the two apart.
лучше (luchshe = better) is the irregular comparative of хороший (haroshiy = good), not a regular ending you can predict.
A possessive matches the noun, not you: книга (kniga = book) is feminine, so my is моя (maya), not мой (moy).
место (mesta = seat) is neuter, so your becomes твоё (tvoyo); masculine would be твой (tvoy), feminine твоя (tvaya).
её (yeyo = her), его (yevo = his), их (ikh = their) never change form, unlike мой (moy) or наш (nash): её платье (platye = dress) keeps её.
The ending -ся/-сь here means it happened on its own: машина (mashina = car) сломалась (slamalas = broke down), nobody broke it.
готов (gatov = ready) is a short adjective for a state, and Russian adds no word for is: заказ готов (zakaz gatov = order ready).
After a comparative you can drop than and put the noun in genitive: теплее весны (teplee vesny = warmer than spring), весна (vesna) becoming весны.
Use свой (svoy) when the owner is the subject: я взял свою книгу (ya vzyal svayu knigu = I took my own book), not мою (mayu).
свой (svoy) means his own here because he is the subject; using его (yevo) would hint the passport belongs to someone else.
With нравится (nravitsya = likes), the person goes in dative: моему другу (mayemu drugu), and музыка (muzyka) is the grammatical subject.
самый (samyy = most) before an adjective builds the superlative and agrees in gender: самый умный ученик (samyy umnyy uchenik = smartest student).
Use чем (chem = than) to compare against an adverb: счастливее (schastlivee = happier), чем раньше (ranshe = before).
